articles.title: Nobel Prize in Medicine 2026: Trio win for breakthrough in optogenetics, unlocking how brain forms memories
articles.summary: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded on Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel \"for their discoveries concerning
articles.body: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded on Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”, a technique that allows scientists to control the activity of nerve cells using light.The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet said the three scientists had laid “the foundation of a new era in neuroscience”. Their work has enabled researchers to switch individual nerve cells on or off in living brains, helping them study how neural circuits control memories, feelings and behaviours.Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2, a light-sensitive protein found in the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas. When exposed to blue light, the protein opens a channel through the cell membrane, allowing positively charged ions to flow in and generate an electrical signal.Karl Deisseroth later transformed this discovery into a tool for controlling nerve cells. In 2005, his research group introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin-2 into rat nerve cells grown in the laboratory. When exposed to blue light, the cells generated nerve signals. In 2007, Deisseroth and his team demonstrated that the technique could be used to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice.The method, which came to be known as optogenetics, has since become a widely used tool in neuroscience. Researchers have used it to identify neural circuits involved in functions including pain, social behaviour, thirst, food consumption, reward and attention, as well as to investigate neurological and psychiatric disorders.“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, said.The work has also opened possible medical applications. Researchers are studying optogenetic approaches to restore vision in people with severe visual impairment, while the technique is also being investigated as a way to improve the precision of cochlear implants.Here is more info about the winners:Karl DeisserothKarl Deisseroth, born in Boston in 1971, is affiliated with the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University in the US. He is the DH Chen Professor and a professor of bioengineering and psychiatry and behavioural sciences at Stanford.Deisseroth received his PhD from Stanford University in 1998 and his MD in 2000. His work has focused on developing tools to understand how specific nerve cells and neural circuits function in the living brain.Peter HegemannPeter Hegemann, born in Münster, Germany, in 1954, is the Hertie Senior Professor of Neuroscience at Humboldt University of Berlin. He received his PhD from the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsried in 1984.Hegemann's interest in how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas senses light led to the discovery of light-gated ion channels. Working with Georg Nagel, he showed that channelrhodopsins could make cells respond directly to light.Georg NagelGeorg Nagel, born in Weingarten, Germany, in 1953, is a professor of molecular plant physiology at the department for molecular plant physiology and biophysics – botany I, University of Würzburg. He received his PhD from the University of Frankfurt in 1988.Nagel played a key role in establishing that channelrhodopsins are light-gated ion channels. By introducing the algal genes into frog egg cells, he and Hegemann demonstrated that the proteins could turn light into an electrical signal in other cells, providing the crucial foundation for the later development of optogenetics.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Germany is at risk': Spy chief warns Russia's shadow war could trigger 'violent' conflict
articles.summary: Germany risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia as Moscow steps up what Berlin describes as an increasingly aggressive “shadow war”
articles.body: Germany risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia as Moscow steps up what Berlin describes as an increasingly aggressive “shadow war” involving espionage, sabotage and other hybrid operations, the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has warned.According to news agency Reuters, Martin Jaeger, head of the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), told lawmakers at the annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs in parliament that the confrontation with Russia had entered a more dangerous phase.“The confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension,” Jaeger said.“Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” he added. “No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany.”Jaeger cited an attempted attack at Leipzig airport in August involving an explosives-laden drone, with Russian agents identified as the prime suspects. German authorities have repeatedly accused Moscow of conducting a hybrid campaign targeting the country and its allies. Russia has denied the allegations.Jaeger said Germany had “become a major obstacle to Russia’s projection of hegemonic power in Europe -- and, consequently, a target of Russian actions”.He said the BND currently sees “no indication” of plans for a major Russian military attack on a NATO member. However, he warned that “low-level Russian military activities could occur, particularly in the Baltic states”.Russia has repeatedly denied any intention of attacking NATO countries."We are not threatening anyone," Russian president Vladimir Putin said on Thursday. "We have no intention of attacking anyone - whether in 2029, 2030 or 2050 - but if we are subjected to aggression, we will have no choice but to respond."The warning came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz travelled to Kyiv on Sunday in a show of support for Ukraine as Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities intensified.“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” Merz said, adding: “You can continue to count on our help.”Germany has provided Ukraine with more than €43.3 billion ($48.8 billion) in aid since the war began and remains one of Kyiv’s largest supporters.Merz and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy also visited a damaged building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in central Kyiv.“These barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are daily war crimes,” Merz said at the site, while calling on Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war.Russia’s foreign ministry, meanwhile, has said it would continue carrying out “mass retaliatory strikes” on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.Germany’s domestic intelligence chief, Sinan Selen, said Russian operations were extending beyond traditional espionage.“Sabotage and assassinations” were increasingly part of the threat, Selen said, adding that “the defence industry and military infrastructure are in the crosshairs”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kelowna grower Jordan Abbate’s giant pumpkin weighed 1,485 pounds at British Columbia’s 2026 contest, beating the 1,484-pound runner-up by just 1 pound after six months of daily care
articles.summary: A giant pumpkin grown by Kelowna resident Jordan Abbate won the 2026 B C Giant Pumpkin Contest in Langley, on Saturday, with just one pound separating the
articles.body: A giant pumpkin grown by Kelowna resident Jordan Abbate won the 2026 B C Giant Pumpkin Contest in Langley, on Saturday, with just one pound separating the top two entries. Abbate’s pumpkin weighed 1,485 pounds, while Team Halliday’s entry came in at 1,484 pounds.The contest was held at Krause Berry Farm in Langley. According to Castanet, Abbate’s win was also a first for the B C Interior, as no grower from the region had previously won the event in its 13-year history.The winning pumpkin was the result of about six months of regular care. Abbate said he spent several hours each day looking after the plant, including watering, pruning and caring for the soil. The work continued even through winter as he prepared the soil for the growing season.Abbate, however, was not very confident about winning before the weigh-off. After learning that his pumpkin had taken first place, he said he was "very satisfied".A global competitionThe B C Giant Pumpkin Contest is the only competition in British Columbia sanctioned by the Great Pumpkin Commonwealth, an international organisation that sets rules and standards for growing giant pumpkins and other oversized fruit and vegetables.The organisation holds about 800 competitions around the world each year. The 2026 event was the 13th B C competition.Contest host Jeff Pelletier had predicted that the scale of the event could lead to records being challenged. "The event gets better every year, and the scale is getting bigger. I believe several B C records will be challenged today, and some may even be broken," he said before the weigh-off, as quoted by Sing Tao Canada Dushi.True to his words, some records were broken during the competition. Although Abbate’s 1,485-pound pumpkin did not set a new B C record, a 1,149-pound giant squash established a new provincial record in its category. Meanwhile, a long gourd measuring 131.5 inches also set a new B C record.The Great Pumpkin Commonwealth recognises eight record categories including giant pumpkin, giant squash, field pumpkin, long gourd, bushel gourd, tomato, watermelon and giant zucchini.Working with the pumpkin for 6 monthsGrowing a pumpkin to this size requires regular attention over a long period. Abbate said he spent several hours every day taking care of the plant during the six-month growing period."It took many months of watering, pruning and taking care of the plant. Even when winter came, I was still working on the soil," he said.The work does not end once the pumpkin begins growing rapidly. According to Pelletier, giant pumpkins need to be checked almost every day during their fastest growth period.They can also gain weight at a remarkable rate. Pelletier said a giant pumpkin can add up to 60 pounds in one day during this stage. "This growth rate will continue for two weeks. For the six months you grow it, it is like your pet," Pelletier said.That rapid increase in size also creates practical challenges. Giant pumpkins and squash can become so heavy that moving them to a weigh-off requires lifting straps and forklifts. For Abbate, the months of work did bear a sweet fruit.Kelowna grower friend wins tooAbbate was not the only Kelowna grower at the event. His friend and fellow Kelowna resident Cassidy Murrell also competed, finishing 10th with a pumpkin weighing 756 pounds.Murrell began growing giant pumpkins about four years ago. He described the hobby as an everyday activity that can take several hours of work.“It’s pretty much an every day hobby,” he said. “I spend at least an hour, maybe even two or three hours a day in the patch. That’s doing everything from pruning to training vines, spraying, fertilizing, checking irrigation, checking on the pumpkin, fighting off the vermin,” Murrell added.The process also involves research before the seeds are even planted. Growers look for seeds with particular lineages, some of which date back to the 1970s and 1980s.Murrell said growers study the history of those lineages to identify traits they want in their pumpkins, including colour and density. They also consider whether a particular lineage is more likely to split.“We use that to determine favourable traits, whether its colour or whether they tend to be denser than other pumpkins. If one lineage tends to split more than others, then we’ll avoid that one. It’s so extensive it’s almost difficult to explain,” he said.Bigger Pumpkin next year?Murrell’s interest in growing giant pumpkins began with his family’s tradition of hosting large Halloween parties. His parents later gave him a gift basket containing a seed-starting tray made by his father. That became the starting point for his own giant-pumpkin hobby.He eventually grew a 70-pound pumpkin and took it to a weigh-off. There, he met Abbate and saw Abbate’s much larger 1,090-pound pumpkin.“I grew a 70 pound pumpkin that I was super proud of, took it to a weigh-off, and that’s when I met Jordan Abbate, with his 1090 pound pumpkin that dwarfed my little 70 pounder,” Murrell said.Murrell now hopes to challenge his friend for the title at Krause Berry Farm. He even supplied Abbate with a seedling this year, turning their friendly competition into another reason to watch next year’s contest. “I gave him his seedling this year, so he better watch out next year,” he joked.Last year, Leif Palmberg and his son Victor from Galiano Island, BC, were placed 1st with their 1,758 pound Giant Atlantic Pumpkin.You use AI every day. articles.title: Exclusive: Soldiers and Gold Star families press Army leadership after deadly Iranian drone strike
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — On a sunny, cloudless morning on March 1, the day after President Donald Trump started the war against Iran, Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — On a sunny, cloudless morning on March 1, the day after President Donald Trump started the war against Iran , Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan was coordinating critical Army supplies out of Port Shuaiba in Kuwait.

In an instant, a drone crashed through the ceiling and exploded, killing Marzan, who had served in the military for 36 years. The force flung soldiers into the air, fragments of sheet metal and glass shards impaling them. The tin roof was peeled back "like opening up a sardine can," one soldier recalled.

Six soldiers were killed and dozens were injured in the deadliest known strike on U.S. troops since Operation Epic Fury commenced on Feb. 28.

For many, the attack at Port Shuaiba has receded into memory as the war nears its eighth month. But to those there that day and their families, it showed the cost of a hastily drawn conflict. The planning had apparent flaws, and commanders did not take intelligence reports of the Iranian threat seriously enough, leaving wounded soldiers questioning Army leadership and the military medical system.

In the aftermath, many of the wounded — some with decades of service and combat experience — told The Associated Press that commanders had been warned that the facility, a rectangular building with wooden sides at a working seaport and industrial area south of Kuwait City, was particularly vulnerable to a drone strike.

That warning went unheeded, the soldiers say. Some also said higher-ranking officers pushed for an all-clear to be called, but it's not certain from their accounts who ultimately made the decision to move soldiers out of a safer space in nearby bunkers. The wounded also would later say their serious injuries were not treated promptly or adequately in the weeks following the attack.

"We have the right to know what really happened," Marzan's widow, Tina Marzan, told the AP. "If somebody messed up, those people need to be held responsible."

Battlefield conditions are inherently chaotic and assessments drawn by those involved are often in tension. The AP's account of the attack is based on interviews with 13 soldiers, primarily officers, serving in key positions of responsibility there or familiar with high-level briefings leading up to the strike.

Along with several Gold Star families — the military's designation for relatives of a soldier killed while on active duty — many are raising their concerns publicly for the first time and calling for the Army to reconcile what they say are failures of preparedness.

Several soldiers spoke on the record, which is rare for troops still in the Army. Others spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. Some details of the attack have been reported by other news organizations, including The Washington Post and CBS News, but the AP is reporting other details for the first time.

In the early days of the war, Trump described it as a "little excursion" that would end quickly but now has no off-ramp in sight. The toll can be measured in 19 U.S. personnel killed, more than 800 wounded and at least $44 billion spent to wage the fight.

The Army declined to comment on the AP's reporting on the Port Shuaiba strike, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack. The Pentagon also declined to comment.

"Out of respect for the primary next of kin who will be scheduled for briefs on the official findings of the completed investigation, we will not comment on specific details, individual accounts, or leaked portions of the report at this time," the Army said in a statement.

The Army completed its investigation of the Port Shuaiba attack in June but has yet to release a report, citing the need to redact sensitive information, said an official familiar with the Army's investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the report has not been released.

Commanding officers followed a familiar playbook

The story of the attack really begins in June 2025, when the U.S. bombed three nuclear sites in Iran . In anticipation of a counterstrike on U.S. troops in Kuwait, military planners relocated soldiers to Port Shuaiba, which the Army used for decades on the belief it was safer.

In the lead-up to the war in February, that was the same playbook followed by Major Gen. John Hinson, the two-star general overseeing logistics for U.S. Central Command in the Middle East, and Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who led the 103rd Expeditionary Sustainment Command, an Iowa-based Army Reserve unit serving a nine-month deployment in Kuwait under Hinson's command. All six soldiers who died, and many of the dozens wounded, were from the 103rd.

Hinson and Barnes chose not to deviate from the plan despite knowing that the port lacked defenses against drones and was seen as increasingly likely to be attacked, according to five officers and an enlisted soldier familiar with the U.S. intelligence and threat assessments. The generals were following orders made at U.S. Army Central, which oversees Army units in the Middle East, and Central Command to leave the nearby Army base, Camp Arifjan.

Hinson declined to comment on the record for this story. Barnes did not respond to text messages and telephone calls.

Even before the attack, the threat of a drone strike was well known. But the command team rejected proposals to move the entire logistics headquarters to other sites identified as safer locations outside Kuwait, farther away from Iran, according to Major Billy Key, an operations planner working for Barnes who has served in the Army for more than 20 years. Another officer confirmed the alternate plans were scuttled. The port was about 65 miles (104 kilometers) from the Iranian border.

"Kuwait was just too close, that's the bottom line," Key said. "Kuwait was in striking distance of low-flying drones."

Senior leadership believed that a core group of the more than 200 soldiers who had been handling logistics at Camp Arifjan needed to remain in Kuwait. Two senior officers, including Lt. Col. Tim Halbur, told the AP that there were communications advantages to being there, so a small crew of about 75 soldiers was sent to the port to set up a temporary field headquarters for logistics in the region. Dozens of troops from other units were also present.

One enlisted soldier, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the command team is facing unfair criticism for hard decisions to balance its ability to carry out a crucial logistics mission with the inherent risks of war.

But six officers told the AP that the logistics headquarters' jobs could have been done from a safer site outside Kuwait, so long as they had access to a secure communications network.

"We did our work on a computer," Key told the AP. "We could have been anywhere."

During meetings, officers overseeing protection told Hinson and Barnes, among others, that Port Shuaiba would not be safe for troops due to the lack of air protection against drones, according to five soldiers who were present: Key, Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom and three others familiar with high-level briefings who insisted on anonymity due to fear of reprisal.

They said the generals were more focused on defending against missiles and were not prepared for drone warfare. "This type of fight has been going on for five years in Ukraine, and our excuse is we didn't expect it to happen to us," Ramsbottom said. "That's preposterous in my mind."

While the three major U.S. military bases in Kuwait had bolstered air protection heading into the war, the only U.S. air support for Port Shuaiba came from a Patriot anti-missile system in the vicinity of Camp Arifjan that was ill-equipped for shooting down Iranian drones.

While the system is capable of detecting the small aircraft, large numbers of drones are able to quickly deplete a battery, and the Patriot missiles cost vastly more than the drones. Using the system to down drones also then leaves the area vulnerable to far more deadly missile attacks.

Neither Hinson nor Barnes was empowered to change anti-air or drone defenses at the site.

"There was nothing that was going to intercept a threat coming at us other than ballistic missiles," Ramsbottom said.

Just days before the relocation to the port in late February, a group of intelligence officers pressed Hinson and Barnes to not go there. Hinson asked whether Port Shuaiba was on a list of planned Iranian targets that had been obtained by U.S. intelligence before Operation Epic Fury and was told that it was not on the list but was considered a likely secondary target, according to two officers familiar with the meeting.

The officers said Hinson still made the call to go.

Lt. Gen. Patrick Frank, then leading Army Central, signed off on the plan to move to Port Shuaiba when Hinson briefed him, Halbur and another senior officer said.

"Obviously, somewhere at the two-star, three-star level, they knew the intelligence reports," Halbur said. "We were just told, like, 'Hey, yeah, we'll be fine there.'"

One officer who was involved in logistics and was wounded in the attack said staying at the Kuwaiti port seemed appropriate. Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón of the Defense Logistics Agency said Port Shuaiba had existing infrastructure for secure communications that could accommodate their unit and Jordan, where U.S. military operations also are based and many soldiers were being relocated, was already getting crowded.

Captain was concerned about port's safety the morning of the attack

At the start of the war, missiles from all sides lit up the screen inside the command post at the port. Soldiers rushed in and out of bunkers. They could feel booms shake the ground.

That night, at least five quadcopter drones hovered over the port and appeared to be surveilling the U.S. military site, according to Key, who said one was only about 40 feet (12 meters) above him. He said he told senior officers what he saw, and it was passed up the chain. "That was the last I heard about it," he added. Intelligence briefings had warned that quadcopter drones were a sign of impending strikes.

The next morning, March 1, Capt. Cody Khork, who oversaw safety for the unit and had strongly advised against going to the port, confided to Ramsbottom that he felt they should not leave their bunker because of the barrage of missiles and drones coming in, according to Ramsbottom. Both Khork and Ramsbottom were concerned that the radar being used to issue all-clears was not picking up low-flying drones.

"We knew we were not safe," said Ramsbottom, who would end up with a piece of shrapnel sticking out of his head and a traumatic brain injury. "No one knew the drone situation."

In the hours before the deadly strike, higher-ranking officers pushed Khork to get troops cleared to leave the bunkers, said Ramsbottom, who was with Khork in the bunker. The team was under tremendous pressure to carry out its mission, which included tracking munitions levels and fuel across the region, and that could not be done from inside the bunker.

It remains unclear who ultimately made the decision to leave the bunkers, which were within several hundred feet of the operations center. Around 10 a.m., about 20 minutes after the final all-clear was issued, an Iranian drone smashed through the operation center's roof.

Ramsbottom and Key recalled the drone struck seconds after Khork passed by them and said "good morning." Key was blasted into a metal cabinet and knocked unconscious. When he awoke, his ears were ringing and he stumbled through the rubble, coming across Khork's lifeless body. A group of soldiers helped take Khork's body from the wreckage to ensure he could be buried with dignity.

Key later recounted the scene to Khork's parents at his funeral in Florida several weeks later, telling them their son appeared to die instantly.

"I would have wanted someone to tell my family that if it were me," Key said. "I felt compelled to tell them exactly what happened."

Lincón, a West Point graduate, remained conscious but was severely wounded by shrapnel and briefly lost his eyesight. Another wounded soldier bandaged him and got him out of the burning building.

"Had it not been for those brave souls, there would have been a lot more, including myself, who probably (would have) burned there in place," Lincón said.

Hinson and Barnes also suffered traumatic brain injuries from the blast, and Hinson's hand was hit with shrapnel.

Planning was limited for a mass casualty event

The soldiers based at Port Shuaiba headed into war without having implemented a broad-based plan for a mass casualty event, seven soldiers, including senior officers stationed there, told the AP. Soldiers who still had their phones intact used Google to locate the nearest medical facilities. Some among the wounded would later say their serious injuries were not treated promptly or adequately in the weeks after the strike.

A medical service officer had prepared an evacuation plan that would have included setting up collection points for transporting wounded soldiers, but she was among the group sent to Jordan, and her plan was never briefed and put into place. She declined to comment.

"I've been in Iraq and Afghanistan. I've been in combat operations before. I know what right looks like, and this was not right by any means," said Chief Warrant Officer 4 Jonathan Tenbrink, who has spent 35 years in the U.S. military and was wounded by shrapnel in his forehead, face, neck, shoulders and right arm.

Relocating to Port Shuaiba, some soldiers acknowledged there was also a false sense of security.

"It was the farthest thing from my mind that we would get hit there," said Lincón, who had deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan multiple times in his 27-year Army career.

A hospital sent wounded soldiers to barracks rather than inpatient care

Even for survivors, there was peril ahead.

Halbur had been among a group of about nine soldiers medically evacuated, and he was having surgery at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland within a week, describing his care there as "excellent." He said he was told by visiting top Army leadership that the Port Shuaiba soldiers were "the guinea pigs" for the medical system as Operation Epic Fury commenced.

But other wounded soldiers, including those with serious head injuries and shrapnel wounds, had vastly different experiences of delayed care after the attack.

One group, some of whom were treated at a Kuwaiti hospital for about 48 hours, holed up in residential homes in Kuwait for another week as Iran unleashed missiles and drones that made it risky for evacuation flights. Soldiers finally boarded a cargo plane flown to Germany.

There, they say, they were not admitted to inpatient care at the military's main medical hub, the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center, but were sent to Army barracks because they had not been documented as combat-injured troops. About a week later they were placed into demobilization at Fort Hood in Texas, a process not focused on providing medical care.

A Pentagon official told the AP that Landstuhl's mission is to stabilize patients to transfer them for specialized care at a military hospital in the U.S., rather than admit them. In a statement, the Pentagon said that all wounded troops who arrive at its medical facilities are evaluated and may be admitted based on the severity of the injury.

Families of the fallen received a briefing

In early July, Gold Star families received a briefing from Frank, who had just ended his rotation as head of Army Central Command, providing a broad overview of the investigation's findings. Tina Marzan said there was no admission of error.

Frank did not say anything about Port Shuaiba's vulnerabilities, only that soldiers were moved around because attacks on other bases were expected, according to Marzan. Frank also told her that there was proper medical treatment available to those at Port Shuaiba, she said.

"Whatever happened unfortunately does not bring my husband back," Marzan said.

One senior officer filed a complaint against Barnes and Hinson to the Army's inspector general. But in a July 20 letter reviewed by the AP, the watchdog concluded that Barnes had not engaged in misconduct or "ignored reliable intelligence" in this complaint based on "the limited evidence" provided by the officer.

The agency also noted this complaint against Hinson was withdrawn, which the officer disputed to the AP. The officer told the AP he relayed his conversations with Barnes discussing intelligence briefings but told investigators he had not directly interacted with Hinson.

Halbur, a father of two from Ankeny, Iowa, had been deployed as an Army reservist seven months earlier, hardly expecting to be on the front lines of a full-blown conflict.

He had served for nearly 30 years, but today he can no longer salute. His dominant right arm will likely never be able to bend past 90 degrees again after the blast shattered his forearm in four places, including his elbow.

"I can't squeeze both arms around my kids because my one arm won't allow me to do that anymore," Halbur said. "I want to coach my son's football team, but at the same time, I can't show them how to throw a football."

He says that his children, age 7 and 8, are coming to learn that "dad's never going to be the same."

He wears the names of the six soldiers who died at Port Shuaiba engraved in a metal wristband: Maj. Cody Khork, 35, an easygoing history buff; Master Sgt. Noah L. Tietjens, 42, a passionate martial arts instructor; Maj. Jeffrey R. O'Brien, 45, a father of three who loved playing the saxophone; Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor, a 39-year-old mother of two with a knack for sarcasm; 20-year-old Sgt. Declan J. Coady, an avid outdoorsman and Eagle Scout; and Marzan, 54, a mentor to many younger soldiers. Khork, Tietjens, Amor and Coady received posthumous promotions.

Halbur said that he looks at the wristband whenever he feels depressed by his arm's limitations.

"I know that there are six families who would give that up in a heartbeat," he said. "So that always kind of gives me a little more motivation to not be so glum about the things that I can't do in my future. I'm still here." ___ Brook reported from New Orleans, Watson from San Diego and Bynum from Savannah, Ga. Associated Press journalists Nicholas Ingram in Ankeny, Iowa, and Thomas Peipert in Colorado Springs, Colo., contributed to this report.

articles.body: PATNA: A five-year-old girl was playing with her toys just a few steps away from her mother’s body, apparently unaware that the woman lying motionless on the bed would never wake up again.The child kept playing inside the house while her 22-year-old mother, Asha Devi, allegedly lay dead after being beaten to death with a stick by her husband.The disturbing incident was reported from Madhurapur Ward 6 under Bidupur police station in Vaishali district.Asha’s family members discovered the alleged murder on Sunday after a local resident called them and informed them that their daughter had died.When the family reached the house, they allegedly found the door open and the house deserted. Asha’s body was lying on the bed, while her five-year-old daughter Anshika Kumari was alone in the courtyard, playing with her dolls.Asha’s father, Ganesh Paswan, said, “the entire family had fled before they arrived, leaving the child alone in the house. The little girl was still calling out for her mother, apparently expecting her to wake up and care for her.”Asha was a resident of Paharpur village, Ward 12, under Jurawanpur police station in Raghopur block of Vaishali. She had married Sujit Paswan, son of Vilas Paswan of Madhurapur village , around two-and-a-half years ago.It was the second marriage for both Asha and Sujit. Sujit’s first wife had died following an illness and had left behind two children. Asha’s first husband had also died of illness, and she had a daughter, Anshika, from that marriage.According to the family, both sides were aware of the children before the marriage. However, Asha’s relatives alleged that the children were frequently a source of disputes between the couple.The family alleged that the couple again quarrelled over the issue on Sunday night, following which Sujit allegedly assaulted Asha with a stick and killed her. The allegations are yet to be independently established by police.Bidupur SHO Ravi Prakash reached the spot with a police team after receiving information about the incident. The police inspected the house and began collecting evidence.“A Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) team has collected evidence from the scene. articles.title: Operation 'Yemen Dawn': Saudi-led coalition joins fight to wrest Red Sea from Houthis
articles.summary: Yemen's internationally recognised government has launched a major military campaign called “Yemen Dawn” against Iran-backed Houthi rebels, with a
articles.body: Yemen's internationally recognised government has launched a major military campaign called “Yemen Dawn” against Iran-backed Houthi rebels, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support as the rebels make fresh territorial gains along the country's Red Sea coast.Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the operation was aimed at “restoring state institutions, liberating" Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-controlled capital, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup.”Saudi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said the coalition was providing “full operational support” to government forces. He said around 100 fighter jets were supporting the campaign and that the coalition had established “air protection” over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.The coalition also claimed to have destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. Those claims could not be independently verified.Why has 'Yemen Dawn' been launchedThe operation follows a rapid Houthi advance in southwestern Yemen and along the Red Sea coastline. The rebels captured the key town of Turbah on Sunday, shortly before the government announced its military offensive.Turbah is strategically important because it lies on the main road connecting Taiz, one of Yemen's most important cities, with Aden, the southern port city that serves as the interim seat of the internationally recognised government.The Houthis had already captured several villages and areas around Taiz. Their latest gains have raised the possibility of the rebels tightening their grip around the city and cutting off routes used by government forces to move troops and supplies.The Institute for the Study of War said the capture of Turbah could seriously restrict the ability of government-aligned forces to reinforce positions around Taiz.“Disrupting resupply has military value, of course, but controlling all the roads in and out of areas to the north of Turbah also prevents government forces from retreating out of the city,” the Washington-based think tank said.Houthis push towards Bab el-MandebThe Houthi advance has also brought the strategically vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait into sharper focus.The rebels made major gains along Yemen's western Red Sea coast in September, capturing the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands. These advances gave them control of Yemen's side of the Bab el-Mandeb, a narrow maritime passage linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.Around 12% of global trade passes through the waterway, making control of the area strategically important not only for Yemen but also for regional and international powers.Saudi-backed forces said on Monday that they had begun attacks on Houthi positions around Dhubab, a coastal town near the strait. The Giants Brigades, a government-allied faction, also announced a “decisive military operation against the Houthi militias” in the Bab el-Mandeb area.Saudi Arabia's intervention marks a major escalation. Al-Malki said the coalition would continue supporting Yemeni government forces until the Houthis are “eliminated.”How did Yemen's war reach this point?The latest escalation follows months of renewed fighting between the Houthis, Saudi Arabia and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government.The current flare-up began in mid-July after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa airport to prevent an unauthorised Iranian flight from landing. The rebels subsequently launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and government forces inside Yemen.They also announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and attacked several Saudi-linked vessels. The fighting intensified in September when the Houthis launched their biggest territorial push in years along the Red Sea coast.Yemen's wider civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis moved south from their northern stronghold, seized Sanaa and forced the government to flee to Saudi Arabia. A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in the conflict.The war has killed more than 150,000 people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.The latest fighting has killed more than 800 people and wounded over 3,600, according to the United Nations. More than 145,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen, while more than 3,000 have fled across the sea to Djibouti.The renewed fighting has also severely affected healthcare in Taiz. Yemen's health ministry, which is aligned with the internationally recognised government, said medical facilities in coastal, western and southern parts of the province had either closed or were functioning only partially.You use AI every day. articles.body: Ukraine's defence ministry on Monday claimed more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity was destroyed by its armed forces."More than 51 per cent of Russia's oil refining capacity is out of action", the ministry said on X.The ministry also reported targeting refineries and processing facilities in Moscow, Yaroslavl, KINEF (Kirishi), Ust-Luga, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran regions, among others during recent attacks.Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy infrastructure in an attempt to curb Moscow's revenue that funds its war campaigns.Ukraine's defence minister Evgeniy Khmara claimed the partial paralysis was a result of carefully planned and systematic work to destroy Moscow's military-economic potential.This is the result of carefully planned, methodical, and systematic work aimed at bleeding the Russian war machine dry and destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said, calling the attacks "a serious blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to wage aggression and to supply its forces."Ukraine increases long-range capabilityAccording to Ukraine’s defence ministry, long-range strike drones have been one of their priorities."This year, we have tripled production and procurement. That is not the limit. Deep strike capabilities will keep scaling", the ministry said."Our deep strikes keep bringing the war onto Russian territory", Khmara said.Last week, Kyiv deployed its home-built ballistic missile "FP-7" in combat for the first time as an affordable alternative to the American supersonic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS).Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the deployment through his post on X."Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result", Zelensky wrote.Russia warns of intensified strikesPreviously, Zelenskyy told Reuters that the forces would "double down" on attacks against Russian oil refineries in response to what he described as a new Russian campaign targeting infrastructure across Ukrainian cities.Russia on Sunday responded that it will intensify strikes on Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine.Russian defence ministry, cited by state-run TASS news agency, said that the Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defence industry sites and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine.Last week, Russia conducted one of its biggest drone and missile attacks on Kyiv's power grid and areas around the region. articles.title: Saudi-led coalition targets Red Sea territory held by Houthis. What's Pakistan's role?
articles.summary: As Saudi Arabia intensifies its military campaign against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, Pakistan's role in the escalating conflict has come under
articles.body: As Saudi Arabia intensifies its military campaign against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, Pakistan's role in the escalating conflict has come under scrutiny.Islamabad has not publicly acknowledged direct involvement in Saudi Arabia's offensive inside Yemen. However, several reports point that Pakistani forces could be helping Saudi Arabia shift more of its military resources towards the war by taking over defensive responsibilities inside the kingdom.That could allow Saudi forces to concentrate on the offensive against the Houthis without Pakistan formally becoming a combatant in Yemen.The issue has gained importance after Yemen's internationally recognised government launched “Yemen Dawn”, a major operation to recover territory seized by the Houthis along the Red Sea coast. Saudi Arabia has pledged “full operational support” to the campaign and says 100 fighter jets are taking part.The coalition has also claimed to have destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets, although those claims could not be independently verified.What exactly is Pakistan doingThe precise extent of Pakistan's involvement remains unclear, with defence analysts assuming that Pakistani forces could take responsibility for air and missile defence, radar, early warning, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-drone operations and electronic warfare inside Saudi Arabia without directly indulding with the Iran-backed Houthis.Retired Pentagon official Dave Des Roches said Saudi Arabia wanted Pakistan to contribute across the “full range of military operations”. But he also said Pakistan was unlikely to accept such an extensive role, with the exact responsibilities and areas of deployment still subject to negotiations.Why Pakistan is unlikely to enter the war directlyA direct Pakistani role in the Yemen offensive would be a much bigger commitment than the defensive support Islamabad appears willing to provide. Pakistan is already trying to balance its obligations to Saudi Arabia with its own security challenges, economic constraints and the risk of being drawn deeper into a regional conflict.Taking over air defence, surveillance or other defensive duties inside Saudi Arabia could free up Saudi forces for operations against the Houthis without putting Pakistani troops directly into combat. Entering Yemen, however, would mean taking on a far more demanding military commitment.Pakistan's own military is already stretched across multiple security challenges at home, while Islamabad is operating under a $7 billion IMF programme and dealing with significant external financing requirements. Its defence spending has risen 18% to PKR 3 trillion, but the government has simultaneously cut federal development spending to PKR 1 trillion.That makes a prolonged overseas campaign difficult to sustain. Pakistan would have to bear the costs of deploying, supplying and rotating troops and equipment in a conflict that could potentially become protracted.Pakistan biting more than it can chew?Pakistan has deepened its security relationship with Saudi Arabia while maintaining important ties with China, Turkey and the United States. Islamabad has also sought to position itself as a mediator in the Middle East. A direct confrontation with the Houthis could complicate that balancing act, particularly given Pakistan's need to manage its relationship with Iran.The financial relationship with Riyadh adds another layer. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly provided Pakistan with financial support, including a $3 billion deposit agreed in April on top of an existing $5 billion arrangement. That gives Islamabad a strong incentive to help protect Saudi Arabia, but it does not necessarily mean Pakistan can afford to fight Saudi Arabia's war directly.Pakistan's own defence spending also puts its limitations into perspective. Its military expenditure stood at $11.9 billion in 2025, far below Saudi Arabia's $83.2 billion.This explains why Islamabad may prefer a carefully defined role that strengthens Saudi Arabia's defensive capacity rather than committing its own forces to the Houthi battlefield.For Pakistan, the calculation is therefore less about whether it can contribute militarily and more about how much it can contribute without turning a strategic partnership into another costly military commitment. A limited defensive role could allow Islamabad to support Riyadh while keeping its own forces out of the Yemen war. A direct intervention, by contrast, risks becoming a case of biting off more than Pakistan can chew.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Gyanesh Kumar must go’: Opposition turns up heat on CEC after SC Form 6 clarification
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Opposition leaders stepped up attacks on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on Monday after the Supreme Court clarified that it had not
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Opposition leaders stepped up attacks on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on Monday after the Supreme Court clarified that it had not approved modifications to Form 6 being used by the Election Commission of India (ECI) during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The INDIA bloc is set to hold a protest march from Parliament House to the Election Commission on Tuesday, with opposition parties demanding accountability over the SIR exercise and raising questions about the functioning of the poll panel.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said the Supreme Court's clarification showed that Kumar had changed Form 6 “illegally and unilaterally”.“It is now established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally. This is just one more proof of him abusing his position to help the BJP,” Gandhi posted on X.He said the CEC and others involved in what he called a “criminal assault on democracy” would be held accountable.Congress leader Pawan Khera said the ECI's earlier justification for the modified Form 6 had now been contradicted by the Supreme Court.“The ECI had sought to justify the controversial Form 6 declaration by claiming that the Form 6 had been upheld by the Supreme Court. That claim has now been squarely contradicted by the Court itself,” Khera said.Samajwadi Party (SP) MP Dharmendra Yadav alleged that no election had been fair under Kumar's supervision and questioned the conduct of polls in several states.“Under their supervision, has any election ever been fair? You tell me, weren't questions raised in Bengal? You tell me, weren't questions raised in Bihar? Weren't questions raised in Delhi? Or didn't the people of Maharashtra raise questions? Didn't the people of Haryana raise questions?” Yadav said.He claimed that five SP seats were “defeated in counting” during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and said the party's performance was not a “favour” from Kumar.“If there hadn't been cheating, 43 Samajwadi Party candidates would have won alone, and our alliance would have won nearly 48 seats,” he alleged.Yadav also said opposition parties would continue their campaign until Kumar resigned.“All those who believe in democracy... such people will make Gyanesh Gupta resign, no matter how many ways of struggle are required, it will be done,” he said.AAP leader Manish Sisodia also targeted Kumar over the Form 6 changes.“The Supreme Court has clearly said Gyanesh Kumar did not get permission to change Form 6,” Sisodia said, alleging that the clarification raised questions over how the changes were made.Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Anil Desai said concerns surrounding the SIR had not been adequately addressed. “Several issues have come to light regarding the SIR, and none of the points raised have been refuted,” Desai said.He alleged that the deletion of voters' names in Maharashtra had caused anxiety and demanded accountability.“The Chief Election Commissioner should accept responsibility for the errors that have come to light and resign. That is why the protest march is taking place tomorrow,” he said.RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav announced an “Akrosh March” at block levels across Bihar on October 7, followed by district-level demonstrations and a march towards the Lok Bhavan on October 8.MAITC MP Derek O’Brien said: “In 2023, a record 146 MPs were unilaterally suspended from Parliament, so BJP could bulldoze CEC Bill which replaced Chief Justice (with a Union Minister) from Selection Committee of CEC & ECs!”“Tuesday, 146+ MPs march in protest from Parliament to EC. GK must GO,” he posted.What the Supreme Court saidA bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, “any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us.”The court was hearing a PIL concerning alleged unilateral decisions related to the SIR. It issued notices to the ECI and Centre but did not pass an interim order restraining Kumar from taking decisions.The opposition's planned march on Tuesday is expected to intensify the political pressure on the poll panel, while the Supreme Court proceedings will determine how the disputed SIR decisions and Form 6 modifications are examined further.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, a Pennsylvania couple accidentally won an abandoned 1830s stone house at auction for $460,000; five years and more than $300,000 in renovations later, the five-acre property is about 85% complete
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring story of Tyler and Lauren Bouldin, a Pennsylvania couple who accidentally won an abandoned 1830s stone house for $460,000 at auction. After five years and over $300,000 in renovations, their property 'The Forge' is now 85% complete. Learn about their challenges, innovative approaches, and dedication to creating their dream home.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania couple looking for a new home where they could raise their growing family ended up buying an abandoned 1830s stone house at auction for $460,000 in 2020.Tyler and Lauren Bouldin, both 36, had originally been looking for a more rural home where they could raise their growing family. After losing several properties in a competitive housing market, the couple began looking for less conventional ways to find a home that fit their needs.That search led them to a five-acre property they called “The Forge”, which Tyler discovered while browsing Zillow, an online real-estate platform.The stone house, surrounded by trees and sitting at the base of a mountain, had the setting the couple wanted. But it also needed extensive work. They toured it twice before the auction and knew they were looking at a major renovation.“We started to realize that we couldn’t afford to buy what we wanted if we didn’t start getting creative,” the couple told PEOPLE.They had no plan to buy a complete remodel, but the property's potential persuaded them to keep considering it.The $460,000 mistakeLauren was out of town when the auction took place, leaving Tyler to attend alone with a firm limit of $440,000.The bidding eventually reached $460,000. According to Lauren's account, Tyler smiled at the auctioneer, who interpreted the gesture as another bid.Just like that, the couple had bought the property for $20,000 more than Tyler's planned maximum.“It was a roller coaster of emotion; at first I just was confused, then thrilled, then panicked, and finally, just excited to call Lauren and tell her that I’d done it,” Tyler told PEOPLE.Lauren's reaction was less about the unexpected price and more about the fact that they had actually secured the property.“When she found out that we’d got it, she was so happy that she cried, which made me cry, and we just had a moment of happy tears together while it all sank in,” Tyler said.The excitement did not last long before the couple had to deal with the condition of their new home.An abandoned house with a bigger problemThe property had been left abandoned and required far more work than the couple initially anticipated.There were missing floors, a collapsing staircase, no kitchen and extensive overgrowth around the property. An abandoned swimming pool presented another problem. It was uncovered and unfenced, filled with dark water and snakes.The couple had expected a substantial renovation, but their original plan was to complete most of the work within about a year by working nights and weekends.That estimate proved unrealistic.“I think we should have been more worried than we actually were, but we had a level of confidence that’s only possible when you don’t know what you’re truly facing,” the couple said.Structural problems, specialist repairs and rising costs after the pandemic disrupted materials and contractor availability pushed the project well beyond its original budget and timeline.Instead of abandoning the renovation, the Bouldins changed their approach.They began reusing materials, searching for cheaper options, taking on more of the work themselves and accepting help from friends, family and people they met through social media.The cost also affected how they lived while the work continued.“We lived with both of our parents at different points to save up money to make this project possible, and gave up five years of eating out, vacations and other lifestyle comforts in exchange for drywall, flooring and late nights working,” the couple said.The snake-filled pool becomes a gardenThe pool was eventually removed rather than restored.The couple demolished it and converted the area into a garden. They also worked to make the surrounding property less attractive to snakes by clearing overgrown areas, removing debris and dealing with rodent habitats.The decision reflected the broader approach they had adopted for the renovation: work with what they had rather than trying to complete everything at once.“You can complete any project by picking two of these three things: good, fast and cheap,” the Bouldins said. “Most of the time, we decided to pick good and cheap if we could — sometimes all we could manage was good, but that’s better than paying a lot for fast.”Five years later, the work continuesThe Bouldins have now spent more than $300,000 on renovations, in addition to the $460,000 they paid for the property.After roughly five years of work, The Forge is about 85% complete.There is still work ahead, including projects involving the roof, windows, barn and chapel, as well as the gardens and other parts of the property.But the couple no longer treats completing the house as a race.“Instead, we focus on being productive when we can, while not losing sight of what’s important to us,” the Bouldins said. “If we rush, overcommit or measure our success by how much progress we’ve made against ‘done’ we’d never be able to enjoy the amazing family and home that we’ve built together!”You use AI every day. articles.title: After 40 days, Nepal ends flood search with 5,285 still missing
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nepal on Monday suspended all non-essential search and rescue operations 40 days after the Aug 26 Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, which left 1,455
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nepal on Monday suspended all non-essential search and rescue operations 40 days after the Aug 26 Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, which left 1,455 people dead and 5,285 missing. It is now shifting focus to reconstruction and rehabilitation. Those still unaccounted for include 189 Indians and dozens of people of Indian origin holding foreign passports.The decision was taken at a meeting of the National Council for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management, chaired by PM Balendra Shah. It followed recommendations from district security and disaster management committees, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and teams that inspected flood-hit areas.The council recommended that the finance ministry approve Nepalese Rs 559 billion (Rs 35,000 crore; $3.6 billion) for 504 reconstruction and rehabilitation programmes submitted by ministries and agencies, with NDRRMA tasked with seeking additional funds for projects whose costs were yet to be assessed. articles.title: 28-year-old Florida woman inherited her late father’s home after caring for him; a 55-plus HOA is now suing to make her leave
articles.summary: Bethany Michel, 28, inherited her late father’s home in a Jacksonville, Florida, 55-plus community after he died in October 2023.
articles.body: Bethany Michel, 28, inherited her late father’s home in a Jacksonville, Florida, 55-plus community after he died in October 2023. Nearly three years into the dispute, the homeowners association is pursuing legal action to remove her because she is below the community’s minimum age for occupancy. Michel said she moved into the Arbor Mill home in 2020 to care for her terminally ill father, a disabled veteran, after COVID-19 restrictions at his assisted living facility made it difficult for her to provide his dialysis care. In July 2026, the HOA approved a $155,000 special assessment, with about $1,000 charged to each household, to help cover legal costs associated with the case. The dispute has divided residents and raised questions about how federal 55-plus housing rules apply when a younger person inherits a home.Bethany Michel inherited the home after caring for her fatherMichel said she moved into the Arbor Mill property during the pandemic while caring for her father. He died in October 2023, after which she inherited the home. Michel said she received notice less than three months after her father’s death reminding her that she did not meet Arbor Mill’s age requirement and asking her to move. The community’s governing documents require every occupied home to have at least one resident who is 55 or older. They also prohibit anyone under 19 from living in the community. The declaration distinguishes between ownership and occupancy, meaning a person under 55 can own a property but may not necessarily be permitted to live in it.Michel has also said her father signed an addendum that included an exception to the community’s 55-plus age policy. PEOPLE reported that it viewed the addendum and said it was unclear whether the document allowed Michel to reside in the home or only addressed her ownership of the property. That distinction is central to the dispute because Arbor Mill’s governing documents separately address ownership and occupancy. The declaration also says the board may grant hardship exceptions to the age requirement at its discretion, provided the community remains compliant with applicable federal fair-housing requirements. The HOA declined to comment on whether it had considered an exception for Michel.HOA approves $155,000 assessment for legal costsThe dispute escalated in July when the Freedom at Arbor Mill Homeowners Association approved a $155,000 special assessment connected to its legal fight with Michel. The amount works out to about $1,000 for each of the community’s approximately 155 households. A notice sent to homeowners before the assessment vote said the $1,000 balance could be paid in full by August 31, 2026, or homeowners could add $100 to their regular monthly assessments for 10 months beginning August 1. Those payment terms were stated in the notice circulated ahead of the vote.Michel used her social media following, which she built partly through restaurant reviews, to draw attention to the dispute. She said residents had been led to believe they would have a direct say on the assessment, but that the five-member HOA board ultimately voted on it. News4JAX reported that the board approved the assessment as part of its continuing legal effort to remove Michel from the community. The assessment has divided residents. Bob Stadler, one of Michel’s neighbours, said he could not afford an additional $1,000 and that many residents live on fixed incomes. William Baltazar also said many residents disagreed with the effort to remove Michel. Other homeowners have argued that the community’s governing documents should be enforced and that the issue is not personal.What federal law says about 55-plus communitiesThe federal Housing for Older Persons Act, or HOPA, allows qualifying housing communities to maintain age restrictions while remaining exempt from the Fair Housing Act’s prohibition on discrimination based on familial status. To qualify under the federal rules, at least 80% of occupied units generally must have at least one resident who is 55 or older, along with other requirements concerning the community’s intent and verification of residents’ ages. That 80% threshold does not mean every 55-plus community must permit younger residents. Communities can adopt stricter occupancy requirements. Arbor Mill’s governing documents require at least one resident aged 55 or older in every occupied home, making its rule stricter than the federal minimum.Alejandra Gonzales, an attorney with Ansbacher Law, told News4JAX that Michel can own the home even if the community’s rules prevent her from occupying it. Gonzales also said the community may already have used its available 20% allowance for residents who do not meet the 55-plus requirement. The reporting does not establish how many younger residents currently live in Arbor Mill. Gonzales said whether the HOA can allow an exception depends on the community’s governing documents and whether doing so would keep Arbor Mill in compliance with federal and state law. She also said an HOA may have authority under its governing documents to impose a special assessment for expenses such as legal fees.Lawsuit was still pending in mid-JulyAs of the mid-July 2026 reporting, the legal dispute between Michel and the HOA remained unresolved. Michel said she had no plans to leave the home and described continuing to live there, including sleeping in the same bed her father used. She has also said she lost access to community amenities including the pool, gym and clubhouse while the dispute continued. The HOA, meanwhile, continued its effort to enforce Arbor Mill’s age-occupancy rules. The case has left residents divided between those who believe Michel should be allowed to remain in the home she inherited from her father and those who believe the community’s 55-plus restrictions should be upheld.You use AI every day. articles.title: Quote of the Day from the Bible: Stop Carrying Tomorrow’s Problems Today; Discover the Powerful Message in Matthew 6:34
articles.summary: It can weigh on you long before tomorrow comes. You are sitting with your family, but your mind is already on an important meeting.
articles.body: It can weigh on you long before tomorrow comes. You are sitting with your family, but your mind is already on an important meeting. You might be chilling out tonight but mulling over next month's expenses. Nothing has happened yet, but the worry has already taken away today's comfort.In those moments, Matthew 6:34 is a powerful biblical lesson on faith, worry, and living in the moment.“Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.”Jesus says that there are enough challenges for each day. You have enough to do, without adding the burden of tomorrow’s difficulties to your responsibilities.Tomorrow's Problems Can Steal Today's PeaceWe humans tend to foresee hurdles. You might not know how your child will perform in the upcoming examination or how the next interview will turn out. When every quiet moment is full of such possibilities, trouble starts.You have to worry about more than today's circumstances. And you're carrying the emotional fallout of things that may never happen. This is another burden that believers must be aware of. Matthew 6:34 says.Planning Is Different From WorryingJesus isn’t telling people to forget about the future. Big responsibilities still exist, like paying the bills, studying for exams, and planning sensibly. The difference lies in the actions that follow reasonable preparation.You don’t have to anticipate all the possible criticism when getting your documents ready for tomorrow’s meeting. You can organise your finances without mentally rehearsing financial disaster all night.Good action is born from planning. Worry often produces the same terrifying thoughts, without change.You Do Not Need Tomorrow's Strength TodayLater on something will come up that you have to be patient, or brave, or make a hard choice. If you think about it all the time, you can start to feel tired before the challenge even begins.Matthew 6:34 brings to our attention the resources available to us right now. You may not have all the answers today, but you can still get the job done with the resources that are immediately at your disposal.No, you don't have to use up the strength needed for the next occasion in advance.Faith Changes Your Relationship With UncertaintyThe bigger lesson of Matthew 6 is about worries over daily needs. Jesus talks about the tendency to get preoccupied with material things: with food and clothing.His message is one of trust. But he is aware of the reality of practical needs. Believers do not believe the future can be fully controlled through constant contemplation, but they can make responsible decisions.Uncertainty may exist, but it need not consume the present.What Matthew 6:34 Asks You to NoticeFacing a challenge is one thing; fantasising about it ad infinitum is quite another. A real challenge may require commitment, help and a sensible evaluation. Sometimes the problem we see can suck the same emotional energy with no concrete benefits.Matthew 6:34 reminds believers that our attention today is on today’s duties. Tomorrow might be a different story, but carrying its weight now, before it arrives, can make a peaceful day feel too heavy.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Pakistani man in Florida creates website to sell fake US postage labels; $100K reward announced for his information
articles.summary: It was a simple but massive fraud. A Pakistani man in Florida operating an unauthorized webiste to sell counterfeit US postage labels has been busted.
articles.body: It was a simple but massive fraud. A Pakistani man in Florida operating an unauthorized webiste to sell counterfeit US postage labels has been busted. 33-year-old Faheem Akram caused the US Postal Services a loss of more than $126 million. According to court records, Akram operated LabelsBank.com, an online website that allegedly sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate, typically $2 per label, regardless of a package’s weight, size, or destination. LabelsBank.com was not authorized to sell USPS products and services. The counterfeit labels allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate USPS prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.“The alleged scheme was simple but massive: sell counterfeit postage online at fixed, cut-rate prices, as little as $2 per label, regardless of a package’s weight, size, or destination, enabling customers to avoid legitimate Postal Service charges,” said US Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida. “The indictment alleges more than 5.1 million counterfeit labels and more than $126 million in losses. Through the work of the US Postal Inspection Service and our prosecutors, the website has been shut down, the domain seized, and federal charges brought against its alleged operator, a Pakistani national.”Quiñones later announced on social media that US Postal Inspection Service was offering a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to Akram's arrest and conviction."We shut down his website. Now we need your help finding him. Faheem Akram is charged with operating a counterfeit postage scheme that allegedly sold more than 5 million fake shipping labels and caused more than $126 million in losses to the U.S. Postal Service. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service is offering a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest and conviction. If you know where he is, call Postal Inspectors at 1-877-876-2455 and say “Law Enforcement.” Do not attempt to apprehend him yourself," the social media post said.The investigation revealed that over 5,200 individuals used LabelsBank.com to purchase more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, resulting in more than $126 million in alleged losses to USPS.Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud. If convicted, Akram faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Misleading': EC fact-checks Rahul Gandhi's 'CEC changed Form 6 illegally' post
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Monday issued a “fact check” amid the controversy over reported changes to Form 6, calling Lok Sabha Leader of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Monday issued a “fact check” amid the controversy over reported changes to Form 6, calling Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s claim that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had “changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally” misleading.In its response, the EC said the order for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Bihar, issued on June 24, 2025, had received the unanimous approval of the Commission and was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in its judgment dated May 27, 2026.The poll panel also cited its Press Note No. 120 dated September 26, 2026, pointing to point 1(iii), which states: “The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.”The EC's response came after Rahul alleged in a post on X that the CEC had changed Form 6 “illegally and unilaterally”, citing the recent Supreme Court observation.EC officials also clarified that Form 6 itself had not been changed, but that a declaration had been attached to the form under the Bihar SIR order, as quoted by PTI.The clarification came after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 used by the EC during the SIR exercise in various states.“Any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it,” a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said.Form 6 is the application used by eligible voters for inclusion in the electoral roll.The declaration was attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR, which began with the EC's June 24, 2025 order. The declaration sought additional details, including information about the applicant's parents.According to EC officials, the form itself remained unchanged, while the declaration was a separate document attached to it for the SIR exercise. Outside SIR, the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 apply.The declaration was later withdrawn from the EC's online portals.The online version of Form 6 and the declaration also used a single OTP for both, rather than requiring separate OTP verification, which had led to suggestions that the declaration was part of Form 6.The EC also rejected claims that it had withdrawn its September 26 press note and shared the document to show that it remained available.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: At a time when there is an escalating debate over AI safety and the power of modern frontier models, an old video of an exchange between Elon Musk and Alibaba co-founder Jack Ma has surfaced online. The video, reposted by Musk, captures Ma doubling down on human exceptionalism, arguing that machines will never outsmart the species that invented them.“Computers may be very clever, but human beings are much smarter. We invented the computer. I've never seen a computer invent a human being,” Ma argued during their conversation at an event in Shanghai in 2019. Ma’s take was rooted in the traditional view of computing: machines are ultimately instruments. While hardware can compute equations faster and store far more data, people retain qualities that silicon cannot replicate, including life experience, nuanced judgment, and wisdom.Ma says computer is one of clever tools humans createdMa, however, acknowledged that AI can beat humans at games like chess and Go but said that computers would remain one of several clever tools that humans have developed.“Don't worry about the machines. For sure, we should understand one thing: that man can never make another man. A computer is a computer. A computer is just a toy. Man cannot even make a mosquito. So, we should have a confidence. Computers only have chips, men have the heart. It's the heart where the wisdom comes from,” he said.He concluded that “my view is that [a] computer may be clever, but human beings are much smarter”.Musk dismissed the premise immediately, posing a direct challenge: “What would be an example of something that humans are better than a computer at?”“It's going to get to the point where [AI] just can completely simulate a person in every way possible, like many people simultaneously. articles.title: IND vs WI: Why India and West Indies were fined after 3rd ODI
articles.summary: India and the West Indies were fined for slow over-rates in the third ODI, with India penalised 20 per cent and the visitors 10 per cent of their match fees....
articles.body:
India and the West Indies have been fined for maintaining slow over-rates during the third and final ODI of their three-match series in New Chandigarh on Saturday. India were four overs behind the required rate after time allowances were taken into account, while the West Indies were two overs short. As a result, India were fined 20 per cent of their match fee, while the West Indies received a 10 per cent fine. "In accordance with Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to minimum over-rate offences, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for every over their side fails to bowl in the allotted time," the ICC said in a statement. Both captains accepted the charges and the proposed sanctions, meaning there was no need for a formal hearing. The penalties were imposed by Prakash Bhatt of the ICC International Panel of Match Referees. On-field umpires Jayaraman Madanagopal and Sam Nogajski, third umpire Sharfuddoula Ibne Shahid and fourth umpire Virender Sharma had levelled the charges.

The West Indies had already lost the three-match series 2-0 before the final ODI, but they finished the series with a memorable win. Led by an unbeaten 162 from captain Shai Hope, the visitors successfully chased down 352, recording their highest successful run chase in ODI cricket. Their previous best was 331/5 against Ireland in 2019.

Hope also created history with his innings. He became the first wicketkeeper-captain to score more than 150 runs in an ODI innings. His knock was also the highest score by a West Indies men's batter in a successful ODI chase, surpassing Brian Lara's 153 against Pakistan in Sharjah in 1993. With the ODI series now over, India and the West Indies will shift their focus to the five-match T20I series, which begins on Tuesday.
